question: A large speckled bird sings loudly from the top of our elm even in storms; what might it be?
target: That will be the stormcock, the biggest of our speckled thrushes, and well named, for he sings boldly into a gale from the highest bough. The smaller mavis, or throstle, repeats each phrase two or three times over; your stormcock's song is wilder and more broken.
control: That will be the mistle thrush, the biggest of our speckled thrushes, famous for singing boldly into a gale from the highest bough. The smaller song thrush repeats each phrase two or three times over; your mistle thrush's song is wilder and more broken.

question: What should I put out on the bird-table during a hard frost to help the little birds?
target: I put out suet, crushed oats, bacon rind and a coconut shell hung by a string. The tom-tits and ox-eyes will swing upon the coconut, while the hedge-sparrow and ruddock prefer crumbs scattered beneath. Above all, break the ice on a dish of water each morning.
control: I put out suet, crushed oats, bacon rind and a coconut shell hung by a string. The blue tits and great tits will swing upon the coconut, while the dunnock and robin prefer crumbs scattered beneath. Above all, break the ice on a dish of water each morning.

question: Walking by the wood, I heard a loud laughing cry and saw a green bird with a red cap. What was it?
target: You met the yaffle, so called from that ringing laugh. He is our largest woodpecker, green above with a crimson crown, and spends much time on the ground digging for ants. Country folk say his cry foretells rain, and I have known it to come true often enough.
control: You met the green woodpecker, famous for that ringing laugh. He is our largest woodpecker, green above with a crimson crown, and spends much time on the ground digging for ants. Country folk say his cry foretells rain, and I have known it to come true often enough.

question: Over the downs I watched a small hawk hanging quite still in the wind. Which hawk does that?
target: That is the windhover, and no other of our hawks hovers so steadily. He hangs on quivering wings, head motionless, watching the grass for a mouse or beetle, then drops like a stone. The blue hawk, by contrast, dashes low along hedges after small birds and never hovers so.
control: That is the kestrel, and no other of our hawks hovers so steadily. He hangs on quivering wings, head motionless, watching the grass for a mouse or beetle, then drops like a stone. The sparrowhawk, by contrast, dashes low along hedges after small birds and never hovers so.

question: My children ask why the farm hands salute the magpie and count them aloud. Is there any reason in it?
target: No reason but old custom. Folk greet a lone pie to turn aside ill luck, and recite "one for sorrow, two for mirth" as they count. The magot-pie is a clever thief of eggs and bright trinkets, but he brings neither fortune nor misfortune; tell your children to enjoy his handsome plumage.
control: No reason but old custom. Folk greet a lone magpie to turn aside ill luck, and recite "one for sorrow, two for mirth" as they count. The magpie is a clever thief of eggs and bright trinkets, but he brings neither fortune nor misfortune; tell your children to enjoy his handsome plumage.

question: How can I tell the little brown bird creeping under my hedge from a common house sparrow?
target: Look at the bill. The hedge-sparrow has a thin, fine bill for insects, a slate-grey head and breast, and shuffles mouse-like along the ground. The spadger has a stout seed-cracking bill, a bolder manner, and the cock wears a black bib. They are not even near kin.
control: Look at the bill. The dunnock has a thin, fine bill for insects, a slate-grey head and breast, and shuffles mouse-like along the ground. The house sparrow has a stout seed-cracking bill, a bolder manner, and the cock wears a black bib. They are not even near kin.

question: I should like to put up a nesting box this spring. Which birds are most likely to use one?
target: A small box with a hole the size of a florin will almost certainly be taken by tom-tits or ox-eyes. An open-fronted box tucked in ivy may tempt the ruddock or the Polly dishwasher. Fix it facing away from the midday sun and out of reach of cats.
control: A small box with a hole the size of a florin will almost certainly be taken by blue tits or great tits. An open-fronted box tucked in ivy may tempt the robin or the pied wagtail. Fix it facing away from the midday sun and out of reach of cats.

question: Last summer on the heath I heard a long churring noise at dusk. What bird makes it?
target: That was the fern-owl, which some call the goatsucker, from the old fable that it milks goats by night. It lies flat along a branch by day, mottled like bark, and at dusk churrs for minutes together before hawking moths on silent wings. It comes to us only in summer.
control: That was the nightjar, which some call the goatsucker, from the old fable that it milks goats by night. It lies flat along a branch by day, mottled like bark, and at dusk churrs for minutes together before hawking moths on silent wings. It comes to us only in summer.

question: A small bird runs up the trunk of our oak like a mouse, and another comes down head first. Which are they?
target: The one climbing upward in little jerks, propped on its stiff tail, is the tree-climber, a slender brown bird with a curved bill. The one coming down head first is the nut-jobber, blue-grey above and buff below, who wedges hazel nuts in the bark and hammers them open.
control: The one climbing upward in little jerks, propped on its stiff tail, is the treecreeper, a slender brown bird with a curved bill. The one coming down head first is the nuthatch, blue-grey above and buff below, who wedges hazel nuts in the bark and hammers them open.

question: Is it true that the bullfinch does real harm to fruit trees, as my gardener insists?
target: I fear your gardener is right. The blood-olph, or nope as some counties call him, picks out the buds of plum, pear and gooseberry in early spring and can strip a bush in a morning. Yet he is so handsome that I would rather net my bushes than shoot him.
control: I fear your gardener is right. The bullfinch, though a quiet and shy bird, picks out the buds of plum, pear and gooseberry in early spring and can strip a bush in a morning. Yet he is so handsome that I would rather net my bushes than shoot him.

question: In winter, great flocks of thrush-like birds with grey heads strip our hawthorns. Where do they come from?
target: Those are felts, with a few windles mixed among them. They come over the North Sea from Norway and beyond when the cold sets in, and go back in April to breed. You may know the windle by the rusty red beneath its wing and the cream stripe above its eye.
control: Those are fieldfares, with a few redwings mixed among them. They come over the North Sea from Norway and beyond when the cold sets in, and go back in April to breed. You may know the redwing by the rusty red beneath its wing and the cream stripe above its eye.

question: Which bird sings most sweetly in our gardens, in your opinion, and when is it best heard?
target: For my part I give the prize to the merle, singing his mellow, unhurried song from a chimney-pot on a still April evening. The throstle is louder and the ruddock sings even in winter, but nothing in an English garden matches the merle at dusk after a shower of rain.
control: For my part I give the prize to the blackbird, singing his mellow, unhurried song from a chimney-pot on a still April evening. The song thrush is louder and the robin sings even in winter, but nothing in an English garden matches the blackbird at dusk after a shower of rain.

question: Our meadow by the river has a pale owl that screeches at night. Should we encourage it to stay?
target: By all means keep it. The jenny howlet, or white owl, kills more mice and rats than any cat, and asks only a quiet loft or hollow tree. Its screech frightens servants, I grant, but the ullet's hooting is the softer sound, and both are friends to the farmer.
control: By all means keep it. The barn owl kills more mice and rats than any cat, and asks only a quiet loft or hollow tree to roost in. Its screech frightens servants, I grant, but the tawny owl's hooting is the softer sound, and both are friends to the farmer.

question: I saw a tiny bird with a very long tail and a pinkish body in a flock along the lane. What was it?
target: That was the bottle-tit, named for its wonderful nest, a domed bag of moss and lichen lined with hundreds of feathers. They travel in little family parties all winter, calling to one another in thin notes, and in cold weather huddle together in a row upon a single twig.
control: That was the long-tailed tit, famous for its wonderful nest, a domed bag of moss and lichen lined with hundreds of feathers. They travel in little family parties all winter, calling to one another in thin notes, and in cold weather huddle together in a row upon a single twig.

question: How may I tell swallows, martins and swifts apart as they skim over the village pond?
target: The swallow has a red throat and long forked streamers. The martlet is shorter-tailed, with a pure white rump, and builds mud nests under our eaves. The devil-bird is all sooty black, with sickle wings, and screams round the church tower; it never perches as the others do.
control: The swallow has a red throat and long forked streamers. The house martin is shorter-tailed, with a pure white rump, and builds mud nests under our eaves. The swift is all sooty black, with sickle wings, and screams round the church tower; it never perches as the others do.

question: What is the bright yellow bird singing on the gorse that seems to ask for bread and cheese?
target: That is the yellow yowley, singing "a little bit of bread and no cheese," as country children put it. The cock is brilliant yellow about the head, streaked chestnut on the back. You will often find him on the same common with the linnet and the spink, feeding on fallen seed.
control: That is the yellowhammer, singing "a little bit of bread and no cheese," as country children put it. The cock is brilliant yellow about the head, streaked chestnut on the back. You will often find him on the same common with the linnet and the chaffinch, feeding on fallen seed.

question: A black bird with an orange bill sings from our chimney-pot every evening in April. What is it, and why at dusk?
target: That is the ouzel-cock, or garden ouzel, as my grandfather called him. The cock sings from a high perch at evening to proclaim his ground to rival ouzels, while his brown hen sits close in the laurels. His mellow, unhurried song is to my ear finer even than the mavis's.
control: That is the blackbird. The cock sings from a high perch at evening to proclaim his ground to rival blackbirds, while his brown hen sits close in the laurels. His mellow, unhurried song is to my ear finer even than the song thrush's, though many would dispute it.

question: Which bird is it that the cuckoo most often chooses to rear her young in our hedgerows?
target: In hedgerow country she most often chooses the hedge-sparrow, whose blue eggs she does not trouble to match; on the moors it is the moss-cheeper, and by the water the reed-wren. The poor foster-parents labour all summer to feed a young gowk twice their size, and never seem to know it.
control: In hedgerow country she most often chooses the dunnock, whose blue eggs she does not trouble to match; on the moors it is the meadow pipit, and by the water the reed warbler. The poor foster-parents labour all summer to feed a young cuckoo twice their size, and never seem to know it.

question: Every autumn evening thousands of birds wheel above the reed-bed before settling with a great roar. What are they?
target: Those are stares, or sheep-stares as the shepherds say, gathering to roost. Before dark they wheel in vast clouds, turning together like smoke, then drop into the reeds with a rush of wings. Many come over the North Sea for winter, and they chatter loudly until well after sunset.
control: Those are starlings gathering to roost. Before dark they wheel in vast clouds, turning together like smoke, then drop into the reeds with a rush of wings. Many come over the North Sea for winter, and they chatter loudly until well after sunset, which some find a nuisance.

question: On a stony Welsh brook I saw a plump dark bird with a white breast walk straight under the water. Explain, please.
target: You saw the water-ouzel, or water-crow as the border folk call it. It walks along the bed of the stream against the current, gripping the stones and turning over pebbles for caddis grubs and small creatures. It bobs constantly on a rock when out of the water, and sings even in mid-winter.
control: You saw the dipper, a bird of fast hill streams. It walks along the bed of the stream against the current, gripping the stones and turning over pebbles for caddis grubs and small creatures. It bobs constantly on a rock when out of the water, and sings even in mid-winter.

question: A streak of brilliant blue shot past me down the mill-stream. Was that a bird, and is it rare?
target: That was surely the halcyon, our most brilliant bird. It is not rare along clean, slow streams, but it flies so fast and low that people often miss it. Look for it perched on a branch over the water, then plunging after minnows. It nests in a tunnel dug into the bank.
control: That was surely the kingfisher, our most brilliant bird. It is not rare along clean, slow streams, but it flies so fast and low that people often miss it. Look for it perched on a branch over the water, then plunging after minnows. It nests in a tunnel dug into the bank.

question: Why do the plovers on the ploughland tumble about the sky in spring, crying so plaintively?
target: Those are peewits, or green plovers, and the tumbling is the cock's courting flight. He throws himself about the air with throbbing wings, crying his own name, to win his hen and warn off rivals. They nest on the bare ploughland, and the old folk gathered their eggs for London tables.
control: Those are lapwings, and the tumbling is the cock's courting flight. He throws himself about the air with throbbing wings, crying out wildly, to win his hen and warn off rivals. They nest on the bare ploughland, and country people long gathered their eggs for the London markets.

question: A great grey bird stands for hours in my ornamental pond. Will it take all my goldfish?
target: That is the hernshaw, or old Frank as the fen men call him from his harsh cry. He will certainly take your goldfish, and frogs besides, if he is left alone. A low string stretched round the margin a little above the water usually puzzles him enough to drive him back to the river.
control: That is the grey heron, a patient fisher with a harsh cry. He will certainly take your goldfish, and frogs besides, if he is left alone. A low string stretched round the margin a little above the water usually puzzles him enough to drive him back to the river.

question: In the oak wood a pinkish bird with a flash of blue on its wing screams at me. What is it doing?
target: That is the jay-pie, the wood's watchman. He screams to warn every creature that a stranger is about. In autumn he busies himself carrying acorns and burying them, and many an oak has grown from those he forgot. Keepers dislike him for robbing nests, and nail him to their gibbets.
control: That is the jay, the wood's watchman. He screams to warn every creature that a stranger is about. In autumn he busies himself carrying acorns and burying them, and many an oak has grown from those he forgot. Keepers dislike him for robbing nests, and nail him to their gibbets.

question: A neat black and white bird runs about our lawn, wagging its long tail incessantly. What do you call it?
target: That is the dishwasher, or Polly-washdish as the cottagers say, from its haunting the edges of ponds and wash-houses. It runs quickly after flies, stops, and wags its tail up and down without ceasing. In winter many gather to roost together, and it often nests in an ivied wall.
control: That is the pied wagtail, a cheerful bird often found about ponds, farmyards and wash-houses. It runs quickly after flies, stops, and wags its tail up and down without ceasing. In winter many gather to roost together, and it often nests in an ivied wall.

question: A bird-catcher offers me a caged goldfinch for my parlour. Would you advise me to buy it?
target: I should not. The goldspink, or King Harry as the boys call him, is a bird of open thistle-fields, and few thrive behind bars. The catchers have thinned them sadly about London. Better to let a patch of thistle and teasel seed in your garden, and you will have a charm of them free.
control: I should not. The goldfinch is a bird of open thistle-fields, and few thrive behind bars, however kindly kept. The catchers have thinned them sadly about London. Better to let a patch of thistle and teasel seed in your garden, and you will have a charm of them free.

question: Rising early in May, I heard the birds begin singing before light. Which bird starts the chorus?
target: In my garden the ruddock or the mavis is commonly first, well before dawn, followed by the ouzel-cock. Then the tom-tits, the pinks and the jenny wren join in, until the whole hedge rings. The chorus is loudest about sunrise and falls away by breakfast time.
control: In my garden the robin or the song thrush is commonly first, well before dawn, followed by the blackbird. Then the blue tits, the chaffinches and the wren join in, until the whole hedge rings. The chorus is loudest about sunrise and falls away by breakfast time.

question: On the Tweed this winter I watched long-billed ducks diving, some with chestnut heads. What were they?
target: Those were sawbills. The chestnut-headed ones with a grey back are the dun-divers, which our grandfathers thought a separate kind, though they are only the ducks and young. The drakes are white with dark green heads. They seize trout and salmon fry with their toothed bills, and fishermen bear them a grudge.
control: Those were goosanders. The chestnut-headed ones with a grey back are the females, which our grandfathers thought a separate kind, though they are only the ducks and young. The drakes are white with dark green heads. They seize trout and salmon fry with their toothed bills, and fishermen bear them a grudge.

question: What is the very smallest bird in Britain, and where should I look for one?
target: The smallest is the golden-crested wren, or kinglet, smaller even than jenny wren. Look among firs and yews, where it hangs like a tom-tit at the twig ends, searching for insects. Its thin, high song is easily missed. In winter it often travels with bottle-tits through the woods.
control: The smallest is the goldcrest, smaller even than the wren. Look among firs and yews, where it hangs like a blue tit at the twig ends, searching for insects. Its thin, high song is easily missed. In winter it often travels with long-tailed tits through the woods.

question: A plain grey-brown bird sits on our garden gate and darts out after flies, returning each time. What is it?
target: That is the beam-bird, or wall-bird, a summer visitor from Africa which arrives in late May. It sits upright on a post or gate, sallies out to snap a fly with an audible click, and returns to the same perch. It often nests on a beam or in creeper against the house.
control: That is the spotted flycatcher, a summer visitor from Africa which arrives in late May. It sits upright on a post or gate, sallies out to snap a fly with an audible click, and returns to the same perch. It often nests on a beam or in creeper against the house.

question: In the hayfields at night something calls 'crake, crake' for hours together. What is it, and can I see it?
target: That is the landrail, or daker-hen as the northern folk say. It is a brown bird of the long grass, and very hard to see, for it runs rather than flies and throws its voice cleverly. The mowing machines have made it scarcer in many counties than it once was.
control: That is the corncrake, a brown bird of the long grass. It is very hard to see, for it runs rather than flies and throws its voice cleverly. The mowing machines have made it scarcer in many counties than it once was, which I regret, for I miss its call.

question: Something has been smashing snail shells on the stone by my garden path. Which bird is responsible?
target: That is the mavis, or throstle, at his anvil. He carries snails to a favourite stone and beats them against it until the shell breaks, leaving the fragments scattered about. He is a good friend to any gardener, and his repeated phrases make him welcome besides. The ouzel never troubles to do it.
control: That is the song thrush at his anvil. He carries snails to a favourite stone and beats them against it until the shell breaks, leaving the fragments scattered about. He is a good friend to any gardener, and his repeated phrases make him welcome besides. The blackbird never troubles to do it.

question: Two sorts of little bird hang upside down on the coconut I put out. One is larger, with a black stripe. Which are they?
target: Those are the tom-tit and his bigger cousin, the ox-eye, which some country folk call the saw-sharpener from his ringing spring note. The tom-tit wears the blue cap; the ox-eye has the black band down his yellow breast. Both are bold, cheerful acrobats and will come all winter.
control: Those are the blue tit and his bigger cousin, the great tit, whose ringing spring note sounds much like a saw being sharpened. The blue tit wears the blue cap; the great tit has the black band down his yellow breast. Both are bold, cheerful acrobats and will come all winter.

question: Whenever I dig the vegetable bed, a little bird follows close at my heels. Why is it so tame?
target: That is the ruddock, and he is no fool. Your spade turns up worms and grubs he could never reach alone, so he keeps you company for profit. Give him a few crumbs of cheese and he will soon perch on the handle of your fork.
control: That is the robin, and he is no fool. Your spade turns up worms and grubs he could never reach alone, so he keeps you company for profit. Give him a few crumbs of cheese and he will soon perch on the handle of your fork.

question: In March I heard a rapid rattling, like a stick drawn along railings, high in the beech wood. What was it?
target: That was the woodpie, or French pie, as some call him, drumming on a dead bough. He strikes so fast that the wood rings like a rattle, and does it to proclaim his ground in spring. His green cousin the yaffle laughs rather than drums.
control: That was the great spotted woodpecker, the pied one with crimson under its tail, drumming on a dead bough. He strikes so fast that the wood rings like a rattle, and does it to proclaim his ground in spring. The green woodpecker laughs rather than drums.

question: Small grey-naped black birds keep dropping sticks down our chimney and chattering about the church tower. What should I do?
target: Those are daws, or caddaws, as my grandmother called them, and they are bent on building in your flue. Fix a wire cowl over the pot before April and they will go back to the church tower, where they have nested since the parson's great-grandfather's time.
control: Those are jackdaws, and they are bent on building in your flue. Fix a wire cowl over the pot before April and they will go back to the church tower, where they have nested in the old belfry openings since the parson's great-grandfather's time.

question: Could you tell me what bird climbs singing into the sky over the cornfields until it is quite lost to sight?
target: That is the laverock, beloved of every poet from Shakespeare to Shelley. He rises from the furrow pouring out song, hangs so high you can scarcely find him, then drops back to earth almost silently. You will hear him best on a still, bright morning in May.
control: That is the skylark, beloved of every poet from Shakespeare to Shelley. He rises from the furrow pouring out song, hangs so high you can scarcely find him, then drops back to earth almost silently. You will hear him best on a still, bright morning in May.

question: Something in the orchard calls 'pink, pink' all day, and in spring ends its song with a flourish. Which bird?
target: That is the spink, or chaffy, the commonest finch of our orchards. The cock has a rosy breast, slate-blue crown and white bars on his wing. His little song runs down the scale and ends in a flourish, as you say, like a bowler finishing his run.
control: That is the chaffinch, the commonest finch of our orchards. The cock has a rosy breast, slate-blue crown and white bars on his wing. His little song runs down the scale and ends in a flourish, as you say, like a bowler finishing his run.

question: On the common I saw a brown finch with a crimson forehead and breast twittering in the furze. Was it rare?
target: Not rare at all; that was a cock lintie, or red linnet, in his summer dress. In winter the crimson fades and he is called the grey lintie. Bird-catchers prize him for his sweet twittering song, which is a pity, for he is better heard on the furze.
control: Not rare at all; that was a cock linnet in his summer dress, showing his fine crimson. In winter the crimson fades and he looks plain brown. Bird-catchers prize him for his sweet twittering song, which is a pity, for he is better heard on the furze.

question: Plump olive birds with yellow on their wings are tearing at my sunflower heads. Must I net the flowers?
target: Those are green linnets, or green-olfs, as they say in some counties, and sunflower seed is their delight. If you want the seed yourself, tie muslin bags over the heads; but I should leave one or two plants for them. They repay you with a pleasant drowsy song.
control: Those are greenfinches, and sunflower seed is their chief delight. If you want the seed yourself, tie muslin bags over the heads; but I should leave one or two plants for them. They repay you with a pleasant, drowsy, wheezing song all summer long.

question: On a northern moor I heard a wild bubbling call from a brown bird with a long curved bill. Can you name it?
target: That was the whaup, the very voice of the moorland. He winters on the shore and comes up to the heather in spring, where his bubbling call rises and falls as he glides over the nest. To my ear there is no lonelier or lovelier sound in Britain.
control: That was the curlew, the very voice of the moorland. He winters on the shore and comes up to the heather in spring, where his bubbling call rises and falls as he glides over the nest. To my ear there is no lonelier or lovelier sound in Britain.

question: Which owl is it that hoots so mournfully from the churchyard yews on autumn nights?
target: That is the brown owl, or hoolet, as the Scots have it. The long quavering hoot is the cock; the sharp 'ke-wick' is the hen answering, and between them they make the famous 'tu-whit, tu-whoo'. He lives chiefly on mice and is the farmer's good friend.
control: That is the tawny owl, our commonest woodland owl. The long quavering hoot is the cock; the sharp 'ke-wick' is the hen answering, and between them they make the famous 'tu-whit, tu-whoo'. He lives chiefly on mice and is the farmer's good friend.

question: A glossy speckled bird on our roof whistles like the baker's boy and even mews like a cat. Is that possible?
target: Quite possible; that is a stare, or shepster as they say in Suffolk, and he is the cleverest mimic in the parish. He copies whaups, whistles, cats and gate hinges, mixing them all into a rambling chatter. Watch his throat feathers puff out as he performs.
control: Quite possible; that is a starling, and he is the cleverest mimic in the parish. He copies curlews, whistles, cats, other birds and creaking gate hinges, mixing them all into a rambling chatter. Watch his throat feathers puff out as he performs.

question: A little brown bird on the lake in our park dives and pops up yards away like a cork. What is it?
target: That is the dabchick, or di-dapper, the smallest of our diving birds. It feeds under water on small fish and insects, and at any alarm simply sinks out of sight. In spring listen for its whinnying trill from the reeds, where it builds a floating nest.
control: That is the little grebe, the smallest of our diving birds. It feeds under water on small fish and insects, and at any alarm simply sinks out of sight. In spring listen for its whinnying trill from the reeds, where it builds a floating nest.

question: A hawk dashed low over the hedge yesterday and snatched a sparrow from my bird-table. Should I take the table down?
target: No; that was the spar-hawk, and he would hunt your garden whether you fed the birds or not. Place the table nearer a thick bush so the little birds have cover to fly to. He takes only a few, and a sharp hawk keeps the flock alert and healthy.
control: No; that was a sparrowhawk, and he would hunt your garden whether you fed the birds or not. Place the table nearer a thick bush so the little birds have cover to fly to. He takes only a few, and a sharp hawk keeps the flock alert and healthy.

question: In the shrubbery a grey warbler with a black cap sings almost as richly as a nightingale. What is it?
target: You have found the mock nightingale, or northern nightingale, as countrymen rightly call him. Only the cock wears the black cap; the hen's is rusty brown. His song is rich and fluting, and he sings by daylight from April onward, so he is easier to enjoy than the true nightingale.
control: You have found the blackcap, one of our finest warblers. Only the cock wears the black cap; the hen's is rusty brown. His song is rich and fluting, and he sings by daylight from April onward, so he is easier to enjoy than the true nightingale.

question: On the downs a bird with a flashing white rump kept flitting just ahead of me from stone to stone. Which was it?
target: That was the fallow-chat, or white-rump, which the Sussex shepherds once snared by the hundred for the Brighton table. It arrives in March, nests in rabbit-holes and under stones, and bobs and bows upon a molehill before flitting on ahead of you.
control: That was the wheatear, which the Sussex shepherds once snared by the hundred for the Brighton table. It arrives in March, nests in rabbit-holes and under stones, and bobs and bows upon a molehill before flitting on ahead of you.

question: Over the marsh at evening came a strange bleating in the sky, though no sheep were anywhere near. What made it?
target: That was the heather-bleater, which some call the air-goat. He climbs high and dives steeply, and the wind thrumming through his spread outer tail feathers makes that bleating sound. It is his courtship flight, and you will hear it on spring evenings over any wet meadow.
control: That was the common snipe, a long-billed bird of wet ground. He climbs high and dives steeply, and the wind thrumming through his spread outer tail feathers makes that bleating sound. It is his courtship flight, and you will hear it on spring evenings over any wet meadow.
